summary: Describes the fixed elements of RFC documents, including title page header, boilerplates, and copyright statements, and updates them for current needs. It also helps handle the separate RFC publication streams. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 7841.

eli5.summary: Every RFC begins with a standard label and legal note, like the front cover of a book. This document explains what goes on the cover and why. It was replaced by RFC 7841.

subtitle: How RFC documents are labeled and what their front matter means.

tldr.problem: RFC documents come from different sources and processes, but readers could not easily tell which is which from the cover page, leading to confusion about an RFC's status and how much review it received.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5741 standardizes the elements of the RFC cover page and boilerplate text, including a line naming the stream (IETF, IAB, IRTF, or Independent Submission) and specific wording to explain each document's origin and approval process.
tldr.outcome: Readers can now understand at a glance where an RFC came from, whether it represents a standard, and what level of consensus or review it received. This document was replaced by RFC 7841.

facts.value: Standards Track, BCP, Experimental, Informational, Historic

facts.value: STD (Standard), BCP (Best Current Practice), FYI (For Your Information)

today: RFC 7841 replaced this document in May 2016, updating the boilerplate text and elements for newer practices.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC documents serve the Internet community in many ways: some define Internet Standards, others offer best practices, and still others share research ideas or historical information. Not all RFCs receive the same level of review. RFC 5741 addresses a practical problem: the front page and boilerplate text of an RFC carry fixed elements that describe its status, but these elements had drifted over time and were not always clear.

The RFC series evolved over decades with different organizations producing RFCs under different review processes. The document defines standard elements for the RFC header and boilerplate to clarify the source of the document and what kind of review it received, so readers are not confused about whether an RFC is a standard they must follow or an interesting but optional experiment.
sections.eli5: RFCs look different depending on who wrote them. This document says what every RFC should have on the front so people know how much to trust it.

sections.title: RFC Streams and Standards
sections.content:
The RFC series includes documents from four distinct streams, each with its own review and approval process. The IETF Stream covers standards track and best practices documents that the Internet Engineering Task Force develops and approves. The IAB Stream includes documents from the Internet Architecture Board, such as informational guidance. The IRTF Stream carries research results from the Internet Research Task Force. The Independent Submission stream is for documents submitted outside these organizations.

It is important to note that not all RFCs are Internet Standards. Some are informational, experimental, or historic. Documents from non-IETF streams are explicitly not reviewed by the IETF for security, congestion control, or interaction with deployed protocols.
sections.eli5: Different groups can write RFCs: the IETF (which writes rules), the IAB (which gives advice), the IRTF (which does research), or anyone else. Each group's RFCs are reviewed differently.

sections.title: The Title Page Header
sections.content:
The RFC header appears at the top of every RFC document. On the left side, it states the document source (the stream name such as IETF or IAB), the RFC number assigned by the RFC Editor, any subseries identifier (like STD for standards or BCP for best practices), the category (Standards Track, Experimental, Informational, Historic, or Best Current Practice), and relationships such as Obsoletes or Updates. On the right side are the authors, their affiliations, and the publication date.

The source line is the most important addition. Historically, all RFCs bore the label "Network Working Group", but this was confusing because it did not indicate where the RFC originated. RFC 5741 replaces this with the actual stream name, so a reader sees immediately whether the RFC is an IETF standard or an IAB recommendation.
sections.eli5: The top of every RFC lists who wrote it, what number it is, and whether it's a rule, advice, or research. The stream name (like IETF) is now clearly shown so you know how official it is.

sections.title: The Status of This Memo
sections.content:
Every RFC includes a "Status of This Memo" section that describes the document's status in three parts. The first paragraph states the category in one sentence (for example, "This is an Internet Standards Track document" or "This document is not an Internet Standards Track specification; it is published for informational purposes"). The second paragraph describes the review process and stream-specific information, explaining who approved it and what level of consensus it has. The third paragraph provides a URL where readers can find errata, current status, and feedback information.

The document gives suggested boilerplate text for each stream and category combination. For instance, IETF Standards Track documents state "It represents the consensus of the IETF community", while IETF Experimental documents may omit this if there was no consensus call. This clarity helps readers understand the weight of the document.
sections.eli5: Right after the title is a paragraph saying what kind of document it is (a rule, advice, research, or history). It explains who checked it and approved it, so you know if it's trustworthy.

sections.title: Other Elements
sections.content:
RFC 5741 also describes other structural elements found in all RFCs: copyright notices that reference BCP 78 and BCP 79 (which define rights and intellectual property), the ISSN number (2070-1721) that uniquely identifies the RFC series, and the positions where the RFC Editor may add additional notes.

The document emphasizes that the goal is to make the RFC structure clear enough that additional notes are rarely needed. The RFC Editor retains responsibility for the exact layout and formatting of these elements, and may adjust details over time via a process documented in RFC 4844.
sections.eli5: RFCs also have copyright and identification numbers. The RFC Editor decides how they are arranged on the page and can change them if needed.
